instructions: Define the final task together: ring a bell, pop a balloon, drop a ball into a cup. Simple finish, complex journey.
Split into teams; each team builds one 'step' of the machine using classroom junk — ramps, dominoes, pulleys, rolling balls.
The rule: each step's output must trigger the next step's input. Teams negotiate the handoff points with their neighbors.
Test each link separately, then run the full machine. It will fail. That's the activity — debug, adjust, rerun.
Film the final successful run. Watch it in slow motion and narrate what each step does.
summary: Teams build one link each of a giant chain-reaction machine — then debug the handoffs until the whole thing runs.
tips: Give it two sessions if you can: build day and debug day. The debugging IS the engineering.
title: Chain Reaction Machines

instructions: Heat water until steaming (adult job) and stir in borax one spoonful at a time until no more dissolves — that's a supersaturated solution.
Pour into jars and add food coloring if you want tinted crystals.
Twist a pipe cleaner into a fun shape (star, snowflake, spiral) and hang it from a pencil across the jar's mouth, fully submerged.
Set jars somewhere they won't be bumped. Check daily and sketch the growth.
In 3–5 days, pull out crystal-covered shapes. Discuss: the cooling water can't hold all the dissolved borax, so it rebuilds into crystals.
summary: Grow sparkling crystals on pipe-cleaner shapes in supersaturated solution — then sketch the daily growth like real scientists.
tips: More borax dissolved = bigger crystals. Keep jars undisturbed; bumps knock crystals off the pipe cleaner.
title: Crystal Gardens

instructions: Fill a big tub or bin with water and lay out 8–10 test objects: a rock, a leaf, a coin, a sponge, an apple, a crayon, a spoon, a plastic cap.
Before each object goes in, every child votes: sink or float? Hands up, count it, record the prediction on a chart.
Drop the object in. Cheer or groan at the result, then mark the chart.
After all objects, sort them: what did the sinkers have in common? The floaters?
Test round two: can you make a sinker float (put the rock in a bowl)? Can you make a floater sink (push the air out of the sponge)?
materials: test objects (rock, leaf, coin, sponge, apple, crayon, spoon, cap)
summary: Predict, test, and chart whether everyday objects sink or float — then try to flip the results.
tips: Towels. Many towels. The prediction chart is what makes it science instead of just splashing.
title: Sink or Float Lab

instructions: Pour whole milk into a shallow dish until the bottom is covered.
Drop 4–5 drops of different food coloring around the milk — don't stir.
Dip a cotton swab in dish soap, then touch it to the milk's surface.
Watch the colors explode outward in swirling patterns. Touch a new spot to trigger it again.
Explain simply: soap breaks the milk's surface tension and chases the fat molecules, dragging color along for the ride.
summary: A drop of soapy cotton swab sends food coloring exploding across milk in marbled swirls.
tips: Whole milk works best — the fat is the fuel. White plates show the colors better than colored ones.
title: Magic Milk Art

instructions: Thread a straw onto a long piece of string and stretch the string tight across the room — tape both ends.
Blow up a balloon (don't tie it) and tape it to the straw, nozzle pointing backward.
Countdown, release, and watch the rocket zoom along the string. Measure the distance.
Experiment: does a bigger balloon go farther? What if you angle the string uphill?
Race round: two strings, two rockets, best of three. Losers explain what they'd change.
summary: Balloons taped to straws become jet-powered rockets racing along strings — Newton's third law you can see.
tips: Long, skinny balloons fly straighter than round ones. Keep the string taut — sag kills speed.
title: Balloon Rocket Races

instructions: Scatter cushions, mats, and foam tiles across the floor as 'safe islands.' Clear a path between them.
Shout 'THE FLOOR IS LAVA!' — everyone has 5 seconds to get onto an island. Anyone touching floor is 'melted' (out for the round, or does 5 jumping jacks to rejoin).
Remove one island each round so it gets harder. Rearrange between rounds.
Variation: call out how to travel — 'hop like a frog to the next island!' 'crab-walk!'
Final round: one island left, whole group must fit on it together for 10 seconds.
summary: Cushions become islands in a sea of lava — hop between them as islands disappear each round.
tips: Set the 'melted' consequence before you start — elimination bores kids fast, but jumping-jack buy-backs keep everyone playing.
title: The Floor Is Lava

instructions: One leader gives commands. Follow them ONLY when they start with 'Simon says.'
Miss a Simon command or follow a fake one? You're out — but you become a 'spotter' who watches for others' mistakes.
Every 2 minutes, rotate the leader so everyone gets a turn being Simon.
Remix rounds: 'Robot Simon' (all moves in slow motion), 'Opposite Simon' (do the reverse), 'Dance Simon' (every command is a dance move).
Finale: the last two players become co-Simons and the whole group plays together.
summary: The classic listening game with remix rounds — robot mode, opposite mode, dance mode — and rotating leaders.
tips: No materials needed, which makes it the perfect filler for any gap in the schedule. Younger kids do better with slower commands.
title: Simon Says Remix

instructions: Crank the music and let everyone dance — silliest moves encouraged, no judgment.
When the music stops, FREEZE. Anyone still moving does a fun 'penalty' (5 spins, a silly face, a compliment to a neighbor).
Each round, add a rule: freeze like a statue, freeze on one foot, freeze as an animal.
Let kids take turns being the DJ who stops the music — they love the power.
Cool-down round: slow song, everyone dances in slow motion, then melts to the floor when it ends.
summary: Dance wild, freeze instantly when the music stops — with escalating freeze challenges each round.
tips: The DJ rotation is what keeps it fresh past round five. Keep penalties silly, never shaming.
title: Freeze Dance Party

instructions: Make a photo list: something that makes you laugh, the tallest thing you can find, a perfect shadow, something blue, your team's best jump.
Teams of 3–4 get 20 minutes and one phone or tablet per team (or the leader's phone, passed around).
Teams sprint around the area capturing every item. Creativity counts double.
Everyone returns and each team presents their 3 best photos on the big screen or passed around.
Vote: funniest photo, most artistic, best team jump. Winners pick the next activity.
summary: Teams sprint around capturing a photo list — funniest, tallest, bluest — then present their best shots for votes.
tips: Set hard boundaries before releasing teams. One device per team keeps it collaborative instead of everyone photographing solo.
title: Photo Scavenger Sprint

instructions: Split into two teams and mark goals with cones or backpacks. Everyone plays in crab position: hands and feet on the ground, belly up.
Drop the ball in the center. Players scoot and kick — no standing up, no hands on the ball (hands are for the ground).
Standing up = free kick for the other team at the spot of the foul.
Play 5-minute halves with a water break. Crab-walking is exhausting — that's the point.
Championship: winners vs. a team of teachers. Teachers must also crab-walk. No exceptions.
summary: Soccer played entirely in crab-walk position — belly up, hands and feet down. Hilarious, exhausting, unforgettable.
tips: Grass or turf only — crab-walking on asphalt destroys hands. Keep halves short; this game is a workout.
title: Crab Walk Soccer

instructions: Make rackets: tape a plastic spoon or ruler to a paper plate, or just use fly swatters.
Blow up one balloon per pair. The balloon is the ball — it floats slowly, so rallies last forever.
Set up a 'net': a line of tape on the floor, a row of chairs, or a string between two tables.
Play first to 5 points. Balloon touches the ground on your side = point for the other team.
Tournament: winners stay on, new challengers rotate in. The balloon never pops mid-rally — that's the beauty of it.
materials: chairs or string for a net
summary: Slow-floating balloons and paper-plate rackets make indoor tennis that never breaks anything — or anyone.
tips: Keep spare balloons handy — they do eventually pop. Underhand 'serves' only keeps rallies going longer.
title: Balloon Tennis

instructions: Build the course with what you have: crawl under tables, hop through hula hoops, balance along a tape line, toss a beanbag into a bucket.
Walk the group through it once slowly, naming each station.
Time each runner individually — or run it as a team relay for bigger groups.
After round one, let kids suggest one change to make it harder. Rebuild and run again.
Record best times on a leaderboard. Revisit the same course next month and watch times drop.
summary: Crawl, hop, balance, and toss through a furniture obstacle course — then time it, tweak it, and beat your record.
tips: Pad sharp table corners before you start. The 'suggest one change' round gives kids ownership and doubles the playtime.
title: Indoor Obstacle Course

instructions: Teach 5 animal moves: bear crawl (hands and feet), frog hops (deep squat jumps), crab walk (belly up), flamingo stand (one leg, 10 seconds), snake slither (belly on floor).
Set up stations or just call them out: 'Everyone, BEAR CRAWL to the wall and back!'
Make it a circuit: 30 seconds per animal, rotate through all five, rest, repeat.
Story mode: narrate a jungle journey and kids move like whatever animal you name in the story.
Cool down with flamingo stands — the balance challenge naturally slows everyone down.
summary: Bear crawls, frog hops, crab walks, and flamingo stands — a full-body workout disguised as a trip to the zoo.
tips: Demonstrate each move first — kids' 'bear crawls' drift toward 'baby crawls' fast. The story mode version holds attention longest.
title: Animal Movement Circuit

instructions: Split into two teams, each with a 'territory' half of the field and a flag (bandana) tucked visibly at the back — not hidden, just guarded.
Players cross into enemy territory to steal the flag. If tagged there, they freeze and must be freed by a teammate's touch.
Carry the flag back to your side to score. Dropped flags stay where they fall.
Play 10-minute rounds, then switch: let teams redesign their defense between rounds.
No guarding within arm's reach of your own flag — that rule keeps the game moving.
summary: Classic capture-the-flag with freeze-and-rescue rules — strategy, sprinting, and glorious last-second steals.
tips: The 'no camping your flag' rule is essential. Play best-of-three rounds so teams can adjust strategy.
title: Flag Tag
